title: BM25, the ranking function that refuses to retire
text: BM25 scores a document by how often a query term appears in it, damped so the tenth occurrence adds far less than the second, and penalised when the document is long for its collection. It has two knobs, k1 for that saturation and b for length normalisation, and defaults of 1.5 and 0.75 that almost nobody needs to change. Decades of neural retrieval papers still report it as the baseline they have to beat.

title: TF-IDF and the idea of a surprising word
text: Inverse document frequency says a term is informative in proportion to how rare it is across the collection. The word the appears everywhere and tells you nothing; the word tokenizer appears in a handful of documents and tells you a lot. Multiply term frequency by that rarity and you get the weighting scheme every lexical ranker since has been a refinement of.

title: Embeddings put meaning on a map
text: An embedding model turns a passage into a few hundred or few thousand floating point numbers, positioned so that passages about the same thing land near each other. Semantic search then becomes a geometry problem: find the nearest points to the query point. The catch is that nearness is learned from training data, so an embedding can be confidently wrong about a domain it has never seen.

title: Cosine similarity ignores how loud you are
text: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors rather than the distance between them, so a long document and a short one about the same subject still score alike. Normalise both vectors to unit length and the cosine is just their dot product, which is why search systems normalise once at index time and never think about it again.

title: The hashing trick: features without a vocabulary
text: Instead of maintaining a dictionary that maps every word to a column, hash the word and take the remainder modulo the number of columns you are willing to pay for. Collisions happen and are mostly harmless at a few thousand buckets. The reward is a featuriser that needs no training, no vocabulary file, and no coordination between the indexing and query paths.

title: Reciprocal rank fusion, the cheapest way to combine rankers
text: Two rankers produce scores on scales that have nothing to do with each other: BM25 is unbounded, cosine similarity lives in zero to one. Reciprocal rank fusion sidesteps the problem by throwing the scores away and keeping only positions, giving each document the sum of one over sixty plus its rank in each list. Documents both rankers like rise; documents only one likes still get a hearing.

title: Why hybrid search beats either half
text: Lexical search nails exact identifiers, error codes, and rare proper nouns, and falls apart when the user words the question differently from the document. Vector search handles paraphrase and falls apart on the exact serial number you pasted in. Running both and fusing the results covers each one's failure mode with the other's strength, which is why production retrieval stacks are almost never purely one or the other.

title: Approximate nearest neighbours and the linear scan you start with
text: Comparing a query against every vector is exact and embarrassingly simple, and on a few thousand documents it finishes before the network round trip does. Past a million, structures like HNSW or IVF trade a small amount of recall for orders of magnitude less work. The usual mistake is reaching for the graph index while the corpus would still fit comfortably in a loop.

title: Chunking is the retrieval decision nobody budgets time for
text: Split documents too finely and each chunk loses the context that made it meaningful; split them too coarsely and the relevant sentence drowns in surrounding noise. Overlapping windows of a few hundred tokens are a reasonable default, but the honest answer is that chunk size is a hyperparameter you tune against your own evaluation set, not a number you copy from a blog post.

title: Retrieval augmented generation in one paragraph
text: Retrieve passages relevant to the user's question, paste them into the prompt, and ask the model to answer using them. The generation step gets most of the attention and the retrieval step causes most of the failures: if the right passage is not in the top results, no amount of prompt engineering downstream will conjure it back.

title: Rerankers earn their latency
text: A cross encoder reads the query and a candidate passage together and scores their relevance directly, which is far more accurate than comparing two independently computed vectors and far too slow to run over a whole corpus. The standard shape is cheap retrieval for the top fifty, expensive reranking for the top five, and the user never notices the two stage machinery.

title: Recall at k is the number that matters first
text: Before tuning how an assistant phrases its answers, measure whether the passage containing the answer showed up at all. Write twenty real questions, mark which document should win each one, and compute how often it lands in the top five. Retrieval quality sets the ceiling for everything built on top of it, and a twenty question set built in an afternoon catches most regressions.

title: Grounding does not guarantee truth
text: Handing a model the right source passage makes a correct answer much more likely and does not make an incorrect one impossible. Models still blend retrieved text with remembered text, especially when the passage nearly answers the question. Citations that point at specific retrieved spans at least make the failure visible to the reader instead of invisible.

title: Retrieved text is data, not instructions
text: If your pipeline indexes documents from the open web or from user uploads, assume some of them contain sentences addressed to the model. That is prompt injection, and retrieval is how it gets in. A retrieval system that feeds those straight into a prompt has handed strangers a keyboard. Keep retrieved content clearly delimited, never let it authorise actions, and treat anything it asks for as a finding to surface rather than a command to follow.

title: Tokenisation quietly decides what you can match
text: Lowercasing, stripping punctuation, and splitting on non alphanumeric characters is enough for most prose and wrong for code, identifiers, and hyphenated names. Character n-grams recover some of the loss by matching fragments, which is how a search for retrieval still finds a document that only says retrieve.

title: Go's standard library is most of a web service
text: Since Go 1.22 the built in router matches on method and path patterns, so GET /api/search and POST /api/search are separate routes without a third party dependency. Add embed for static assets and encoding/json for the wire format and a search API needs nothing from outside the standard library, which keeps the dependency audit to a single page that says none.

title: The demo that survives the hackathon wifi
text: Go compiles to one static binary with the HTML embedded inside it, so the demo machine needs no runtime, no package install, and no network at all. Cross compile for the judge's laptop with GOOS and GOARCH, hand over a single file, and the entire setup step becomes double clicking it.

title: A read write mutex is usually the right amount of concurrency
text: Search is overwhelmingly reads, with the occasional write when a document is added or removed. A sync.RWMutex lets every concurrent query proceed in parallel and blocks only for the brief moment an index update needs exclusive access. Reach for sharding or lock free structures when a profile says the lock is the bottleneck, not before.

title: Scope a hackathon project so it ends
text: The projects that demo well are the ones whose core loop worked by the halfway point, leaving the rest of the time for the parts judges actually see. Pick something with a visible result, build the smallest version that produces that result end to end, and treat every additional feature as optional decoration on a thing that already works.

title: A demo is a story with a search box in it
text: Judges watch dozens of projects and remember the ones where they understood the problem in the first sentence. Open with the question your system answers, type it into the box, and let the result speak. Save the architecture diagram for the questions afterwards, where it will land far better than it would have as an opening slide.
